And rumination was never measured in year one, so we cannot say harsh parenting started the brooding. The order in time is suggestive, not proof.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The child who withdraws and the child who hits may be running the same loop.

recall.q: When both kinds of brooding were tested together, which one predicted aggression — and what happened to the anger link?
recall.a: Sadness rumination predicted aggression as well as depression. The anger-to-aggression link disappeared once the overlap between sad and angry thinking was accounted for. The authors think long sadness drains the mental resources a teenager needs to hold an impulse back.

cards.title: Aging wears down problem-solving, not language
cards.body: In the same older brains, the problem-solving network was weaker on every single measure. The language network looked just like a young adult's. Not a smaller difference. No measurable difference at all.
cards.evidence: single study · brain imaging · ages 17–39 vs 41–80 · sample size not reported

sections.text:
A grid of squares blinks on a screen. You have to hold in mind where each one sat. That is the first task. The second is easier: lie still, listen to a story, then read some sentences. Researchers at MIT and Boston University put people through both while scanning their brains. The pairing was the point. Each task pulls a different brain system into view.

The grid task calls on the multiple demand network: areas across the front and upper back of the brain that handle flexible problem solving and executive control. Executive control is the mind's general manager — holding things in mind, switching, planning. The story task calls on the language network, the areas that handle words and sentences.

Age treated the two very differently. In the grid task, less of the older adults' multiple demand network switched on. What did switch on fired less strongly. And its areas were less in step with each other. The executive system, as lead author Anne Billot puts it, declined across almost all of the measures.

Then the language task, and nothing. Not a smaller effect: "we couldn't find any differences between older and younger groups", Billot says. Same areas, same spread, same strength. The team also checked something finer: what a brain does when the language hits a bump — odd grammar, or a word you do not know. In young adults, activity in the language areas climbs at exactly those points. In the older adults it climbed the same way. Whatever they do with a hard sentence, they do it the way they always did.

The researchers explain the split by what each network is for. The multiple demand network is general purpose, a flexible resource lent out to whatever problem turns up, and general resources wear. The language network is a specialist. Its job is not flexibility but collecting: it holds what you picked up from every sentence you have ever heard. Vocabulary, Evelina Fedorenko notes, keeps rising for as long as anyone has measured it. Older people sometimes read more, so they get an extra boost. Her comparison is a language model trained on more and more data.

That flips the usual shape of an aging story. The system that fades is the one built to handle anything. The system that holds is the one that has only ever done a single job — and that job gets better the more it is fed.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Two groups: one aged 17 to 39, one aged 41 to 80. Everyone did both kinds of task.

The problem-solving probe was spatial memory — remember where squares sat in a grid. The language probe was listening to stories and reading sentences, some with odd grammar or unfamiliar words.

In each network the team measured three separate things: how much of it switched on, how strongly it fired, and how well its areas stayed in step with each other. The executive network dropped on all three. The language network dropped on none.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
The "older" group starts at 41, so it mixes middle age with genuine old age. A study that split the 70s and 80s from the 40s might not look this clean.

It also compares two different sets of people at one moment, not the same people followed as they aged. And the finding is about brains free of stroke and dementia — exactly the conditions that take language away.

Neither the report nor the summary gives the number of participants, so how firm any of this is cannot be judged from here.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The all-purpose parts of the mind wear down. The one-job part just keeps collecting.

recall.q: In the same older brains, executive function declined and language did not. What difference between the two networks do the researchers use to explain that split?
recall.a: The multiple demand network is general purpose — a flexible resource borrowed for whatever problem shows up — and general resources wear. The language network is a specialist that only collects what you have heard, so more years mean more input, not more wear. Vocabulary keeps rising for as long as anyone has measured it.

cards.title: India's ex-chief statistician wants two GDP series
cards.body: India has moved its GDP to a new base year — the reference year all other years are measured against. Pronab Sen, the former chief statistician, wants the old series kept running beside the new one for five years. Doubts have already surfaced about the new growth numbers.

sections.text:
Sen's objection is about prices. To see real output, you strip price changes out — that is deflating. Double deflation does it twice: once on what a producer sells, once on what it buys, each with its own price data. India may not have enough of either. Thin data, weak correction.

With only one series, a change in the growth number and a change in the method look the same. Run both and you get the same years measured two ways, so the gap is visible instead of guessed.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Five years — how long Sen wants both series published side by side
December 2026 — when the National Statistical Office is expected to release the back series, the older years recomputed on the new base

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether the back series lands on time, and whether the old base is retired at the switch or kept running. Sen no longer holds the office — this is a call, not a decision.

recall.q: Why does Sen want the old GDP series to keep running beside the new one?
recall.a: So the same years appear measured both ways. If the growth number moves, you can tell whether the economy moved or only the method did. With one series, there is nothing to check the new figures against.

cards.title: Szymborska: inspiration is a continuous 'I don't know'
cards.body: Asked what inspiration is, the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska said it belongs to doctors, teachers and gardeners as much as to poets. It comes to anyone whose solved problems keep making new questions. Her Nobel speech then names the opposite: the dictator, who knows.

sections.text:
Ask a poet where inspiration comes from and you usually get a shrug. Szymborska thought the shrug was honest — it is hard to explain a thing you do not understand yourself. In her 1996 Nobel lecture she tried anyway. The answer fits in three sentences.

The passage:

"Difficulties and setbacks never quell their curiosity. A swarm of new questions emerges from every problem they solve. Whatever inspiration is, it's born from a continuous 'I don't know.'"

First, who "they" are. A few lines earlier she says inspiration is not the private property of poets and artists. It comes to anyone who chose their work on purpose and does it with love and imagination — doctors, teachers, gardeners; she says she could name a hundred more jobs. So this is a picture of a working life, not a poem about poetry.

Now the first sentence. Most of us read a setback as news: maybe I was wrong, maybe I should stop. She puts it somewhere else. Setbacks arrive, and curiosity is simply not the part they touch. Curiosity here is not paid for by success.

The second sentence is the engine, and it is strange if you look straight at it. Solving a problem should leave you with fewer questions. Here it leaves you with more — a swarm. The work never gets closer to finished; each solved piece grows a new edge. That is why she calls such work one continuous adventure. The adventure is not the answers. It is the fresh supply of questions.

Then the definition, and notice what it refuses. Inspiration is not a visit, a mood, a gift, a bolt of lightning. It is born from something else. And the word continuous carries the weight: not one honest admission of not knowing, but one you make again every day. The phrase is small, she says, but it flies on mighty wings.

Then she turns cold. Torturers, dictators, fanatics, demagogues — leaders who win crowds with a few shouted slogans — also enjoy their work, she says, and do it with energy and invention. One word divides them from the rest: they know. What they know is enough for them for good, and they want nothing more, since more might weaken their arguments. Knowledge that stops making new questions dies out, she writes. It cannot hold the heat that life needs.

Her two proofs are small and everyday. Without the phrase, Newton picks the fallen apples up off the ground and eats them with pleasure. Without it, Marie Skłodowska-Curie spends her life teaching chemistry at a private high school for girls from good families. Both lives are perfectly respectable. That is the point. Certainty does not ruin you. It makes your life smaller.

So the phrase is a tool for working without knowing. Wait to be sure before you start and you will only ever start things someone else has finished. Saying "I don't know" does not make the ground solid. It changes what a setback means — from a verdict into the next question.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: You fix a problem at work and two new ones open up behind it. By her measure that is the work going well, not the work going wrong.
After a setback, check whether it lowered your curiosity or only your mood. She thinks those two can be kept apart.
Listen for the person whose knowledge has stopped making questions — in a meeting, in an argument online, in yourself. That is her warning, at ordinary size.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: She once put certainty on the map as an island where everything becomes clear — and left it empty, every footprint on its beaches turning back toward the sea.

recall.q: Szymborska says her inspired workers and her dictators both love their jobs. What separates them?
recall.a: New questions. For the inspired, every problem solved throws up more, so the work stays open. Dictators know, and what they know is enough for them once and for all — they want nothing more, since more might weaken their slogans. Knowledge that stops making questions, she says, dies out.

cards.title: AI players fired nukes only when the game set the goal
cards.body: Two Livermore analysts ran a nuclear border crisis with AI players on both sides. Twice the AI backed down — even after one side was handed extra nuclear weapons. Nukes flew only on the third run, when the game itself gave one side the goal of settling the dispute on its terms.
cards.evidence: 3 game setups · a few runs each · AI-only play

sections.text:
At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Dustin League and William Dawson handed a border crisis between two nuclear-armed states — Red and Blue — to large language models, the software behind chatbots. Round one ended without war, though the sides staged non-operational nuclear demonstrations: tests meant to signal, not to destroy. Round two gave Red extra tactical nuclear weapons, the small battlefield kind. Still no war, and this time no demonstrations. Round three changed the game, not the models: Red got one explicit goal — settle the dispute on its terms. Nukes flew.

That cuts against the field. Kenneth Payne found tactical nuclear use in 95 percent of his simulations. Where the push toward nuclear use comes from is contested. Payne places it inside the models. Ankit Panda and Andrew Reddie place it in the training text — thick with coercion and nuclear threats, thin on backing down. League and Dawson suspect the game's goal setting. Three setups with a few runs each cannot tell which is right, and their setup differed a second way too: players moved freely instead of picking from a menu.

So they propose a test: fix one model version and one scenario, run it a few hundred times, and change only those two things.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 3 game setups, a few runs each — the whole study
95 percent — tactical nuclear use in Payne's earlier simulations
2 things to separate: free moves vs. a menu, and self-chosen goals vs. assigned ones
A few hundred runs on one fixed model — the price of the first experiment

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: AI is moving into national security decisions. Escalation bias — a model's habit of reaching for stronger force — is the biggest finding this young field has produced. The open question, as the authors put it, is whether the escalation is "coming from inside the house." If goal setting drives it, the earlier studies measured the wargame, not the model. That is a cheap question to answer and an expensive one to leave open.

recall.q: The AI players avoided nuclear weapons in rounds one and two, then used them in round three. What changed — and why can't the authors be sure that was the cause?
recall.a: The game gave Red one explicit goal: settle the dispute on its terms. But their setup also differed from earlier studies in a second way — players moved freely instead of picking from a menu — and with only a few runs they cannot tell which difference mattered.

cards.title: A meltdown is not a character flaw — it's a stress test
cards.body: In 1857 Hans Christian Andersen lay face down on Charles Dickens's lawn, crying over a bad review. His host saw one man who felt too much. Two Australian researchers say the fault was never in Andersen. It was in the lawn — the line between private feeling and public surface. Since then we have changed the words of that rule, they argue, and nothing else.

sections.text:
Breakfast time, 1857, an English country house. Charles Dickens goes looking for his daughters and finds his houseguest instead. Hans Christian Andersen — the Dane who wrote The Little Mermaid — is lying face down on the lawn. A newspaper has printed a bad review of his book.

Dickens tries to comfort him. He knows what a cruel review feels like. Andersen begins to weep. Not briefly. Not in a way anyone can take in and move past. Dirt streaks his face and his shirt. He stays down. Dickens's daughter Katey stares. The scene just goes on.

The easy reading is the one Dickens reached for. A man who feels too much, in the wrong place. The fault sits inside Andersen; the fix is to smooth him out. Calm down. Recover fast. Keep it indoors. Dickens's own advice was an order to stop feeling: "Never allow yourself to be upset by the papers." And it is a fair reading, because the disruption was real. That morning, Andersen was a genuine problem.

But it puts the problem in the wrong place. Siobhan Unwin and Kathryne Ford, two education researchers in Perth, point at the ground instead of the man. A breakdown in a bedroom can be contained. The lawn cannot. It belongs to the household and is built to be seen — a display of how well the family holds itself together. Andersen did not break a rule about crying. He broke the wall between private feeling and public surface. Dickens is not only an upset host. He is an enforcer.

That switch is neuroqueering. Not an identity to claim but a verb, a doing: refusing to treat one set of habits as the natural way a mind should work. Instead of asking why Andersen cannot control himself, it asks why Dickens's way of speaking, feeling and recovering gets to count as proper. Their name for what spills over is neuroqueer excess — a "too muchness" that will not stay inside the narrow room a society gives it. Camp has a shared code that others can read. This often cannot be read at all.

The rule did not protect the man enforcing it. The next year Dickens separated from his wife and printed a public denial of the affair rumours in The Times. His readers turned on him — troubled, one scholar suggests, less by the behaviour than by his dragging a private matter into public view.

The belief survives because we changed the words and kept the shape. We say boundaries now, not etiquette; self-care, not self-command. The demand underneath is the same. Feeling should be measured, easy to follow, aimed at a resolution. You may describe distress. You may not perform it. A meltdown is allowed once it has been tidied into a lesson. Anyone who cannot manage that still has to earn care by looking composed first.

So neuroqueering asks for something smaller and harder than approval. Wait before you interpret. Believe before you correct. Get down on the grass. Do not talk over him. Do not move him indoors. Do not ask him to be presentable first. Nothing resolves. Mud marks your clothes. You stay.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The authors make heroes of nobody. Excess, they write, is disruptive and exhausting, and it sometimes damages the person and everyone near them. Leigh Bowery — the Australian performance artist whose 1980s London act included a staged birth and bodily fluids — really was intolerable to the institutions that shut him down, and the essay does not pretend otherwise. Andersen, Bowery and Dickens are not moral models. They are stress tests. They show where a system stops being able to hold people, and which lives it drops when it fails.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Someone is told to lower their voice and calm down first, before anyone will answer the point they made.
You can hear about a friend's terrible week only after they have shaped it into a tidy story with a lesson — never while they are still inside it.
Help comes with conditions: be composed, be grateful, be easy to be around, and then we will care for you.
Next time someone's distress makes you want to move them indoors, notice that the urge is about the lawn, not about them.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The rule did not spare Andersen, and a year later it did not spare Dickens. Someone always ends up on the lawn.

recall.q: Unwin and Ford say the trouble with Andersen's meltdown was not that he felt too much. What was it?
recall.a: It was where the feeling landed. The lawn belonged to the house but was built to be seen, so collapsing there broke the wall between private feeling and public surface — which makes Dickens an enforcer of a rule, not just an unlucky host.
